data.title: Seatriumâs slowing order book weighs on sentiment despite improving margins
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Analysts are mixed on Seatrium’s prospects after its third-quarter business update, as a slowing order book overshadows improving project margins and cost savings.

CGS International (CGSI) downgraded its call on the offshore, marine and energy specialist to “hold”. UOB Kay Hian (UOBKH) kept its “hold” rating, while DBS and OCBC maintained their “buy” calls.

Seatrium’s share price has slumped more than 10 per cent in the last five trading sessions amid overall global market weakness, hitting a 52-week low of S$1.49 on Monday (Nov 23) morning.

It later recovered to S$1.53 after the midday break, though it was still down 1.9 per cent on the day at that level.

On Nov 19, Seatrium reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending to 2033. It also said it had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year.

The group expects the momentum in Q3 to last till the end of the year, adding that underlying net profit for FY2026 would be “materially higher” than for the previous year.

Order book momentum a concern

CGSI trimmed its target price for Seatrium to S$1.80 from S$2.60, citing “slower-than-expected order win momentum, which dampens (its) earnings expectations”.

The brokerage lowered its FY2027 and FY2028 core earnings forecasts by 11 per cent, incorporating “a lower order win assumption for 2026”.

CGSI flagged upside risks, including order wins such as the award of the final Golar contract, further gas-related orders and another high-voltage direct current order from European transmission operator TenneT.

Downside risks, meanwhile, include delayed order wins, unfavourable outcomes of litigations and cost overruns.

DBS Group Research was the most bullish among the four brokers, maintaining its “buy” recommendation and S$3 target price.

Analyst Ho Pei Hwa noted that Seatrium’s “margin recovery progresses alongside strong execution”. She added that Seatrium’s business update points to “steady operational performance, with revenue maintaining its run rate and gross margins improving relative to the first half of 2026”.

“The near-term earnings trajectory is constructive, but sustained order replenishment remains essential to translate margin recovery into durable growth,” she added.

Recent share price dip offers buying opportunity

OCBC was also upbeat, keeping its “buy” rating with an unchanged fair value estimate of S$2.62.

It said the “recent share price weakness offers accumulation opportunity”, noting that Seatrium’s management remains “confident of order replenishment but is explicitly prioritising profitability over volume”.

“The improving profitability outlook should support its valuation expansion”, it added.

UOBKH kept its “hold” rating on the stock while lowering its target to S$1.80 from S$2.30. “Seatrium needs some sizeable contract wins in the next few months to bolster investor confidence,” it noted. The brokerage flagged Seatrium’s weak order book as a “key issue”, pointing to the decline from S$17.8 billion as at end-2025. The current order book provides “very limited revenue and earnings visibility”, it said. UOBKH also pointed out that more than 70 per cent of Seatrium’s net order book value comes from projects with delivery dates extending beyond 2029, so a sizeable portion of the value from those projects is unlikely to be billed to customers in the next two years.

data.title: Trump hosts gala for meme coin investors as his token plunges to record lowsÂ
data.description:
[NEW YORK] US President Donald Trump has made hundreds of millions from his $TRUMP meme coin, but at a Sunday (Nov 22) dinner for the token’s biggest holders, he said his motive for supporting the cryptocurrency was to boost the economic competitiveness of the United States.

“I’m doing it for the United States... If we don’t do it, China’s going to do it,” Trump told attendees at his golf club outside Washington.

It was the third time Trump had held a gala for the top owners of his meme coin, which once soared as high as US$75 but has fallen to a record low of under US$1.

The private dinner this year was more low-key than the initial event last year, attendees said, with a smaller crowd and far less money at stake this time. Attendees qualified for the dinner based on their time-weighted holdings of the $TRUMP coin from Sep 30 to Nov 16.

Organisers indicated that 185 crypto wallets met the criteria for Sunday’s dinner, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets when the contest concluded on November 16.

Together, those listed wallets only held US$8.6 million – a shadow of the US$148 million listed for the dinner in May 2025, which was attended by 220 wealthy crypto investors.

Sunday’s participants stood in the rain as they waited to enter the Trump National club in Sterling, Virginia. Attendees described the scene inside as subdued.

It was a far different atmosphere from the first gala, when tuxedo-clad contest winners pulled up to the club in luxury sports cars, and protesters chanted and stomped outside the club as the presidential Marine One helicopter descended.

The May 2025 event’s biggest $TRUMP holder was China-born crypto billionaire Justin Sun, who had US$18.5 million of the token. This time, there was no Sun at the event signing autographs.

Attendees were able to dine on grilled filet mignon and pan-seared halibut while hearing speeches from the likes of Kevin O’Leary of the Shark Tank television show and NBA veteran Tristan Thompson.

According to the contest’s website, the top 29 winners would join a VIP reception with the president and receive a gift bag with Trump swag. The top four also would get an 18-karat gold Trump-branded watch.

Morten Christensen, founder of cryptocurrency platform Airdrop Alert, said he qualified for the top 29 with US$41,000 of time-weighted $TRUMP holdings by using a hedging strategy – buying and selling the token using perpetual futures – that ensured he did not lose any money.

But he was denied a VIP band at the event, Christensen said.

“I asked like five people from the staff” and was told to email customer support, he said on Sunday night.

“Obviously, no one is going to reply right now,” said Christensen, who added that he was kicked out of the event around 7 pm for “sharing with the press.”

He waited outside in the rain for his sister, who was still inside.

The Trump Meme Coin project and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Meme coin tumbles

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than US$5 billion, according to a Reuters analysis.

But the $TRUMP token has earned the Trump family itself at least US$635 million, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement.

In total, the Trumps had earned at least US$2.3 billion through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about US$430 million. REUTERS

data.title: Chinaâs record state fund rescue masks deepening investor gloom
data.description:
CHINA’S state-backed funds poured a record amount of money into the market on Friday (Nov 20) in another forceful attempt to stem a deepening sell-off. 

Inflows into the nine exchange-traded funds (ETFs) known to be actively traded by the so-called national team totalled 90 billion yuan (US$13.5 billion) on Friday, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

That surpassed the previous high of 87 billion yuan during the rout in April 2025 spurred by US tariffs. The Harvest CSI 300 ETF drew a record 23 billion yuan, while the ChinaAMC SSE 50 ETF attracted an all-time high of 21.7 billion yuan.

Beijing has intensified efforts to restore confidence after a months-long rout pushed the CSI 300 Index into a bear market, stepping up ETF purchases and easing margin-financing rules.

The measures have yet to put a floor under the market, with various indicators suggesting investor sentiment has failed to improve despite headline benchmarks being propped up with national team buying.

“I’m not sure we’ve hit rock bottom,” said Li Ying, a fund manager at Shanghai Zhenying Investment Management.

“Turnover has shrunk dramatically, but we haven’t seen the widespread margin calls typical of historical troughs, and some of the remaining trading activity is still being supported by the national team.”

On Sunday, authorities lowered the minimum requirement for investors buying securities with borrowed funds to 80 per cent from 100 per cent.

Still, the onshore benchmark fell as much as 1.3 per cent on Monday. The gauge has fallen in all but two weeks since August.

Market breadth remained weak, with the share of stocks trading above their 200-day moving averages slumping on Friday to just 8 per cent in Shenzhen and 12 per cent in Shanghai, the lowest since just before Beijing’s sweeping stimulus package in September 2024.

Technical indicators also show that losers are increasingly outnumbering winners.

Purchases of ETFs by the national team have mostly been confined to late-session buying that supports headline indices such as the CSI 300 while providing little lift to the broader market.

That contrasts with other parts of the market that typically receive less state support, with the small-cap CSI 2000 Index tumbling 14 per cent last week amid the global sell-off. 

Short positions have climbed to around 30 billion yuan, the highest since July 2024, when regulators imposed new restrictions on short selling and made the trade more expensive.

While securities lending from China Securities Finance has yet to resume, the outstanding value of short trades has continued to rise, reflecting growing demand for hedges as the market’s sell-off deepens. 

Meanwhile, leveraged buyers are pulling back. The outstanding balance of margin trades dropped by 1.9 per cent on Friday, the fastest pace of decline since Jul 20.

Authorities have also cut borrowing costs for corporate share buybacks and provided liquidity for financial institutions to increase stock purchases. But take-up of the buyback facility has remained muted. BLOOMBERG

data.title: National Australia Bank speeds up layoff talks after e-mail blunder
data.description:
NATIONAL Australia Bank (NAB) was forced to bring forward conversations with employees affected by planned layoffs, after it inadvertently told some staff that they were being let go ahead of a formal communication.  

The bank had sent the e-mail on Monday (Nov 23) to staff who had already chosen to leave as part of a recently announced restructuring. The e-mail was not intended to be sent before employees learnt directly about the outcome of the process, NAB said. 

The message notified them that their system access would be turned off on Dec 2, the Australian Financial Review reported earlier. The staffers were meant to meet with their managers this week to ascertain if they would still have a job or receive a payout, according to the publication.  

“We are very sorry this happened, and that receiving an automated e-mail this way would be upsetting and unsettling to many,” NAB said. “This is not the experience we wanted any colleague to have, and we sincerely apologise for the distress this error has caused to any who received these e-mails.”   

NAB is planning to cut up to 2,500 jobs as part of an overhaul to navigate heightened competition, a sluggish economy that has weakened home lending and rapid technological change, it said last month.

The process to exit workers has run into mishaps when firms botch the process. In 2025, rival ANZ had to accelerate planned layoffs after automated e-mails were mistakenly sent to some employees before they were told of their termination. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Vietnam picks French-Korean group for high-speed rail deal
data.description:
VIETNAM has selected a consortium of eight French, South Korean and Vietnamese contractors for a 10.24 trillion dong (US$399 million) contract for surveys, feasibility study and design for the North-South high-speed railway, one of the country’s flagship infrastructure projects.

The consortium, led by France’s Systra, includes three South Korean firms: Sambo Engineering, Yooshin Engineering Corp and Korea National Railway, according to the Vietnamese Ministry of Construction’s news website. The project management board aims to sign a contract with the group this month. 

Under the 30-month agreement, the group will conduct surveys and a feasibility study, carry out front-end engineering design and prepare bidding documents for the construction phrase, state media reported. The work will help determine the project’s technology and investment options, providing the technical basis for subsequent implementation. 

The decision marks the first concrete step in Vietnam’s push to build a roughly US$65 billion high-speed railway linking Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, a project expected to reshape transport and economic links along the length of the country.

Construction of the planned line, one of the nation’s biggest-ever infrastructure undertakings, was delayed by a year until the end of 2027 after Vietnam said in September that implementation has been slower than expected.

The group, which includes four Vietnamese companies, is tasked with identifying the route and key locations, including railway stations, bridges and tunnels. Their interim report, due within the first year, must outline technology options for the government to consider and approve. 

The study must meet technical requirements while minimising disruption to local development plans and residents’ daily lives, the Ministry of Construction said. Thousands of people are expected to be relocated from their land to make way for the new line. 

Vietnam’s parliament on Saturday (Nov 21) passed land law amendments aimed at speeding up site clearance for projects, including the expropriation of land in ​the case of some special projects, as the government targets economic growth of at least 10 per cent this year.

When completed, the high-speed rail project is set to have a total length of about 1,541 km and reduce the journey time from the current 30 hours to around five. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Around two-thirds of Singtel SDS holders choose to hold their shares as scheme concludes
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singaporeans who had bought Singtel special discounted shares (SDS) and left them in their CPF accounts will now be able to manage their shares directly through their Central Depository (CDP) accounts.

Singtel and the Central Provident Fund Board announced on Monday (Nov 23) that they completed the transfer of SDS on Nov 21, ending the CPF Board’s legacy role as the trustee of the shares.

Around 209,000 SDS holders, or 34 per cent, had sold their Singtel SDS before the transfer. The remaining SDS, amounting to 477 million held by about 406,000 holders, were transferred to their CDP accounts.

Around two-thirds of SDS holders who kept their shares already had individual CDP accounts, while the remaining one-third had their shares automatically transferred to designated CDP accounts created in their names.

SDS holders who also own Singtel ordinary shares will have both sets of shares consolidated in the same CDP accounts for ease of management, the telco said.

The SDS scheme was introduced in 1993 as part of the Government’s efforts to give Singaporeans a stake in the Republic’s economic success through share ownership.

Singtel was the first and only company to offer SDS shares when it transitioned from a statutory board to a listed company that year.

The CPF Board was appointed as trustee to facilitate the share purchase, as share ownership was still a foreign concept among many Singaporeans at the time.

Today, with stock market trading ubiquitous, the SDS scheme has met its intent and the trustee arrangement to support share ownership is no longer necessary, CPF said in April, when the decision to end the scheme was announced.

SDS holders were thus allowed to sell their shares for cash or wait for their shares to be transferred.

According to Singtel data, the median Singtel SDS holder owns 1,360 shares at an average purchase cost of S$2,000. At April’s market price of around S$5 per Singtel share, those shares would have been worth about S$6,800.

Parliament subsequently approved the CPF Amendment Bill in May to formalise the winding down of the scheme.

Singtel and the CPF Board advised SDS holders to remain vigilant against scams and to verify the URL of the SDS website to ensure it is the official one.

CPF monies withdrawn by members, including any SDS sale proceeds refunded to their Ordinary Accounts, will be credited to their bank accounts registered with the CPF Board.

If they suspect they have fallen for a scam involving their CPF savings, they should get their bank to freeze their bank accounts, reset their Singpass password, and activate the CPF Safety Switch to immediately cease any unintended monetary outflows.

Singtel group chief financial officer Arthur Lang said in a statement: “Over the past several months, our focus has been on ensuring SDS holders had the information, resources and support needed to navigate this transition with confidence, and we are pleased that the transfer has been completed smoothly.

“This initiative was ultimately about giving SDS holders a choice and enabling them to exercise their rights as shareholders directly.”

He added that Singtel now has greater flexibility to engage its shareholder base, execute corporate actions and allocate capital in ways that enhance growth and shareholder returns.

Singtel shares opened 1.4 per cent lower at S$4.11 when the market started trading on Monday. The telco’s shares have fallen around 17 per cent since April. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Consider lowering homeownership barriers for some non-resident foreigners
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore has a high homeownership rate; about nine in 10 resident households own their homes.

However, people living and working here who are not Singapore citizens or permanent residents face huge obstacles when buying a home.

A non-PR foreigner buying any home pays 60 per cent additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD). ABSD does not apply to a citizen buying a first home, while a PR first homebuyer pays 5 per cent ABSD.

ABSD is paid in addition to buyer’s stamp duty, which is progressive and ranges from 1 to 6 per cent for homes.

The Republic is open to skilled foreign professionals; this enhances its attractiveness as a location for high value-add activities, and in turn supports better job opportunities for Singaporeans.  

The Employment Pass (EP) allows foreign professionals, managers, executives and technicians to work here. 

As at June 2026, there were 204,300 EP holders, up from 203,300 as at December 2025. Among the EP holders are people who have been living here for several years or more, and have not been able to secure PR status. 

In perspective, a PR buying a first home for S$2 million pays ABSD of S$100,000, while an EP holder purchasing a home of similar value may have to pay ABSD of S$1.2 million.

Lower ABSD rates

Should transaction costs for EP holders buying homes here be lowered? Perhaps, for first home purchases, levy ABSD of 10 per cent on EP holders who have held such status for over three consecutive years.

Singapore is competing for high-quality foreign talent, especially in fast-growing or critical parts of the economy where there is a shortage of talent.

Letting an EP holder buy a home here without facing swingeing transaction costs could enhance the Republic’s attractiveness to skilled foreigners.  And the stickiness from owning a home might better anchor EP holders to the country. 

Moreover, it would appear fair for an EP holder – who has spent multiple years here – to not face far higher transaction costs than a PR, when buying a first home here for owner occupation.

Importantly, too, some non-PR foreigners buying a first home here for investment might not pay any ABSD. 

Under respective free trade agreements (FTAs), nationals and PRs of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland as well as US nationals are accorded the same stamp duty treatment as Singapore citizens.

In short, a US citizen buying a first home here need not incur ABSD, for example.

Should EP holders from other countries pay much higher transaction taxes on first home purchases than nationals of the above countries with FTAs?

An EP holder who spends around S$6,000 a month in housing rent would incur about S$864,000 in rental expenses over 12 years. Using some or all of these funds to help buy a home here instead, should transaction costs not be punitive, can be enormously helpful to the said EP holder.

Over a 12-year period between Q3 2014 and Q3 2026, the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s property price index of private homes rose by about 50 per cent, while the rental index of private homes islandwide climbed by around 43 per cent.

HDB ownership restrictions

Another key difference in the housing market between PRs and non-PR foreigners is in Housing & Development Board (HDB) flat ownership.

For example, a couple comprising partners who have held PR status for at least three years can buy a HDB resale unclassified or standard flat, excluding 3Gen flats, whereas non-PR foreigner households cannot own HDB flats.

Consider allowing a couple, both EP holders, who have held such status for at least three years, to buy HDB resale unclassified or standard flats excluding 3Gen units. Perhaps, apply a resale levy to said EP holders when they sell their HDB units.

Having PR and other foreigner households live within HDB estates can possibly help such households better assimilate with Singaporeans.

Also, consider expanding public housing options for couples comprising a Singapore citizen and a non-PR foreigner.

Numerous Singapore citizens marry non-PR foreigners. In 2025, the number of marriages involving a citizen and a non-resident foreigner was 5,909. There were marriages involving a citizen and 4,189 non-resident brides, as well as 1,720 non-resident grooms.

Currently, subject to meeting various criteria, a couple comprising a Singapore citizen and a non-PR foreigner who holds a valid work pass or visit pass, and is hoping to buy a new HDB flat, is restricted to buying a two-room flexi unit.

In this case, the citizen looking to purchase a new HDB flat must be at least 35 years old. New HDB flats, unlike resale units, are sold at subsidised prices.

Possibly, lower the age requirement to buy a new HDB flat for a Singapore citizen who marries a non-resident foreigner spouse. Also, subject to meeting various criteria, let a couple comprising a citizen and a non-resident buy larger new HDB flats.

A larger two-room flexi flat is about half the size of a four-room flat. The former has one bedroom, while the latter has three bedrooms.

Rightly, housing policies here prioritise Singapore citizens over PRs and PRs over non-PR foreigners.

Indeed, a key perk for a rich foreigner becoming a Singaporean is the right to buy a home here cost-effectively. A newly minted citizen can buy a landed property including a detached house in a Good Class Bungalow Area. Ownership of landed homes, meanwhile, is generally restricted to Singapore citizens.  

Hopefully, the Republic draws foreigners to become PRs and citizens, for reasons beyond just gaining Singapore citizenship or PR status which offers a cost-effective way to homeownership in safe haven Singapore.  

Having foreigners who become Singaporeans because they treasure and contribute to the nation’s multiculturalism, social cohesion, rule of law, strong work ethic and economic dynamism among others would be great.

Meanwhile, let us be more welcoming to non-resident foreigners such as EP holders, and those who marry Singaporeans by easing homeownership barriers for EP holders, as well as couples comprising a citizen and a non-resident spouse.

data.title: How will the world change after the China-US-Russia summit?
data.description:
ON NOVEMBER 19, China, the United States and Russia held their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen. The meeting was undoubtedly of considerable geopolitical significance.

Leaders of three countries with enormous influence on international affairs, yet profound strategic differences, had finally sat down at the same table.

Afterwards, Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin issued a joint Peace Declaration, pledging to safeguard world peace and promote strategic stability among major powers.

They agreed that “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”.

The Shenzhen summit has inevitably invited comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain and then-Soviet Union discussed the post-war international order.

However, the two meetings took place in fundamentally different geopolitical circumstances and carried very different historical implications.

At Yalta, the three powers were wartime allies fighting against fascism, and their discussions involved shaping the post-war order and determining spheres of influence.

That arrangement reflected the reality of great-power dominance over smaller countries.

Today’s China, US and Russia, by contrast, have no comparable alliance foundation. Instead, they face deep strategic disagreements.

China has consistently emphasised the interests and representation of the Global South, arguing that international affairs should not be determined by a handful of major powers.

It would therefore be misleading to interpret the Shenzhen summit as a new Yalta-style arrangement for dividing the world.

Is a new pattern of relations emerging?

Rather, Shenzhen’s significance lies in establishing a channel for major-power communication and managing differences in an increasingly interconnected world.

The summit’s greatest achievement may not be any sudden resolution of conflicts, but the common signal that strategic competition must not spiral out of control.

Competition between China and the US in technology, trade and industry will continue, as will the tensions between Russia and the West.

Yet, all three powers share certain interests, including preventing military conflicts, reducing nuclear risks and maintaining stable energy supplies.

The world may therefore be witnessing the emergence of a new pattern in relations among major powers, where competition will be long-term, cooperation selective, and strategic stability a public good that all sides need.

For the global economy, the Shenzhen summit’s immediate outcomes may be limited. It has reduced the likelihood of worst-case scenarios – much like installing a “shock absorber” in the global economy rather than fitting it with a new growth engine.

Asian countries are watching

For Asia, this shock absorber matters particularly.

Asian businesses increasingly have to consider geopolitical risks alongside costs, markets and technology when making investment decisions.

Tariffs, export controls and tensions among major powers can raise financing costs, delay investment and disrupt supply chains.

If the Shenzhen summit leads to sustained channels of communication, it could improve the long-term investment outlook – particularly for infrastructure, energy, advanced manufacturing and cross-border logistics.

Stable energy supplies are particularly important to energy-importing Asian economies. If better coordination among major powers could translate to a more predictable external energy environment, it would be an ideal outcome.

More importantly, the summit could create greater room for Asean to exercise strategic autonomy.

More stable relations among major powers would help Asean maintain its openness and flexibility in international economic engagement.

Amid growing US-China competition, Asean countries do not want to be forced to choose sides or lose access to the markets, capital and technology of either power.

However, Asean should not assume that improved communication among major powers will automatically remove geopolitical risks.

Implications for Asean

The region’s strategic autonomy will ultimately depend on strengthening its own economic capabilities, industrial capacity and institutional competitiveness.

This is particularly relevant to the changing nature of China-Asean economic relations, where cooperation is moving beyond trade in consumer goods towards deeper integration of industrial supply chains and productive capacity.

Chinese investment, machinery, technology and industrial intermediate goods are increasingly supporting the development of manufacturing industries in Asean.

This offers regional economies opportunities to upgrade their industrial capabilities and move into higher-value segments of global production networks.

Yet deeper Asean-China integration also brings new challenges.

If Asean manufacturers rely heavily on the US market while using Chinese industrial inputs, their exports could face greater exposure to US tariffs, rules-of-origin scrutiny and trade restrictions.

Asean countries should therefore continue to diversify their export markets, to include China, the 15 signatory countries of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and other Global South economies.

Technology competition presents another challenge, especially as artificial intelligence has become a focal point of US-China strategic rivalry.

US restrictions on advanced semiconductors and computing capabilities could affect Chinese companies’ investments in data centres and AI infrastructure in South-east Asia.

Asean should pursue a diversified, open and rules-based AI ecosystem, moving beyond the construction of computing infrastructure towards developing practical AI applications and regional digital cooperation.

From a broader perspective, Asia as a whole has the opportunity to become an important organiser of a new form of globalisation, one that seeks a new balance between security, efficiency and resilience.

Asia can play a greater role in connecting production capabilities, technology and markets across borders.

Of course, Trump, Xi and Putin cannot determine the future of the world economy at a single summit.

What matters now is whether they can sustain high-level communication and translate political declarations into practical cooperation.

For Asia and Asean, perhaps the summit’s greatest value lies in their willingness to prevent differences from escalating into confrontation.

In an uncertain world, sometimes preventing a crisis is an economic achievement.

However, Asean should not assume that improved communication among major powers will automatically remove geopolitical risks.

Implications for Asean

The region’s strategic autonomy will ultimately depend on strengthening its own economic capabilities, industrial capacity and institutional competitiveness.

This is particularly relevant to the changing nature of China-Asean economic relations, where cooperation is moving beyond trade in consumer goods towards deeper integration of industrial supply chains and productive capacity.

Chinese investment, machinery, technology and industrial intermediate goods are increasingly supporting the development of manufacturing industries in Asean.

This offers regional economies opportunities to upgrade their industrial capabilities and move into higher-value segments of global production networks.

Yet deeper Asean-China integration also brings new challenges.

If Asean manufacturers rely heavily on the US market while using Chinese industrial inputs, their exports could face greater exposure to US tariffs, rules-of-origin scrutiny and trade restrictions.

Asean countries should therefore continue to diversify their export markets, to include China, the 15 signatory countries of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and other Global South economies.

Technology competition presents another challenge, especially as artificial intelligence has become a focal point of US-China strategic rivalry.

US restrictions on advanced semiconductors and computing capabilities could affect Chinese companies’ investments in data centres and AI infrastructure in South-east Asia.

Asean should pursue a diversified, open and rules-based AI ecosystem, moving beyond the construction of computing infrastructure towards developing practical AI applications and regional digital cooperation.

From a broader perspective, Asia as a whole has the opportunity to become an important organiser of a new form of globalisation, one that seeks a new balance between security, efficiency and resilience.

Asia can play a greater role in connecting production capabilities, technology and markets across borders.

Of course, Trump, Xi and Putin cannot determine the future of the world economy at a single summit.

What matters now is whether they can sustain high-level communication and translate political declarations into practical cooperation.

For Asia and Asean, perhaps the summit’s greatest value lies in their willingness to prevent differences from escalating into confrontation.

In an uncertain world, sometimes preventing a crisis is an economic achievement.
